set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with chest pain after a car accident that killed her sister has ST elevation and an elevated troponin; stress cardiomyopathy is suspected. Her pain has eased and she is hemodynamically stable in the emergency department. Which disposition is most appropriate?
opts: Admit to cardiology

Correct. Because Takotsubo mimics acute coronary syndrome with no reliable early differences, patients are admitted to cardiology and managed on acute coronary syndrome protocols with supportive treatment.
Discharge home today
Discharge would be unsafe while she cannot be told apart from an acute coronary syndrome. The management calls for admission to cardiology.
Outpatient follow-up only
Outpatient follow-up would miss the need for acute coronary syndrome evaluation. Suspected stress cardiomyopathy is admitted to cardiology.
Refer for transplant listing
Transplant listing is for refractory end-stage disease. Most patients with stress cardiomyopathy recover completely and are admitted to cardiology.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy comes to clinic with mild breathlessness on exertion. Her examination shows trace ankle edema and clear lungs. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 60 pg/mL. What does this natriuretic peptide result indicate?
opts: Myocarditis is confirmed
Myocarditis is established by endomyocardial biopsy once other causes are excluded; a natriuretic peptide does not confirm it, and hers is below the exclusion cut-off.
Filling pressure is raised
Raised filling pressure releases B-type natriuretic peptide and pushes the level up. A result under 100 pg/mL points the other way and excludes heart failure.
Heart failure is excluded
Correct. B-type natriuretic peptide is released when ventricular filling pressures are high, and a level below 100 pg/mL excludes heart failure as the explanation for her current symptoms.
Heart failure is confirmed
An elevated B-type natriuretic peptide indicates raised left ventricular filling pressure and dysfunction. A level of 60 pg/mL is below 100, which excludes heart failure.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man has stable dilated cardiomyopathy of two years' duration with no systemic illness and no recent change in his heart function. He has read about heart biopsies online and asks whether he should have one. What is the role of a heart muscle biopsy for him?
opts: Not routine and rarely useful

Correct. Biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is rarely useful. Its indications are a recent onset of rapidly deteriorating function or a systemic disease that can involve the heart.
Required to confirm every case
Dilated cardiomyopathy is diagnosed with echocardiography, electrocardiogram, radiograph and laboratory tests; biopsy is not required and is kept for rapid deterioration or systemic disease.
The gold standard for his disease
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not for stable dilated cardiomyopathy, where it is rarely useful and not done routinely.
The first test before echocardiography
Echocardiography comes first and shows the dilated, thin-walled ventricle. Biopsy, if ever used, is reserved for rapid deterioration or suspected systemic disease.

set1.q: A 25-year-old woman has newly diagnosed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a septum of 2.2 cm and occasional palpitations. Her cardiologist wants to judge her risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Which test assesses that risk?
opts: A repeat chest radiograph
The chest radiograph may be normal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and says nothing about arrhythmia. Ambulatory monitoring for 24 to 48 hours assesses that risk.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring
Correct. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours should be performed in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to assess the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is not required for diagnosis and is kept for when a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Arrhythmia risk is assessed with ambulatory monitoring.
A genetic testing panel
Genetic testing is available but does not influence treatment, and it does not grade her arrhythmia risk. Ambulatory rhythm monitoring does.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman is recovering in hospital from stress cardiomyopathy that followed news of her son's serious illness. Her chest pain has resolved, and she asks whether her heart will stay damaged. Which answer about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Poorest outlook of any type
The poorest prognosis among heart muscle diseases belongs to restrictive cardiomyopathy. Stress cardiomyopathy usually resolves completely.
Most patients recover completely
Correct. Takotsubo is a transient regional systolic dysfunction, and most patients completely recover, which distinguishes its prognosis from the progressive cardiomyopathies.
Half die within five years
Fifty percent mortality at five years describes symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy. Most patients with stress cardiomyopathy recover completely.
It always progresses to failure
The dysfunction in Takotsubo is transient, and most patients recover completely rather than progressing to chronic heart failure.

set1.q: A 27-year-old man admitted with presumed viral myocarditis keeps deteriorating despite full medical treatment. Coronary angiography is normal, and valvular, toxic and ischemic causes of heart failure have been excluded. Which test establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Serum troponin
Troponin indicates myonecrosis but does not identify its cause. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard that establishes myocarditis.
Endomyocardial biopsy

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis once other causes of heart failure are excluded, and it is recommended for acute deterioration of unknown origin that does not respond to treatment.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization and angiography are used to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new heart failure, and his were normal. Biopsy is what establishes myocarditis.
Chest radiograph
The chest radiograph in myocarditis is nonspecific and may only show cardiomegaly. The gold standard is endomyocardial biopsy.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman received mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy for a chest cancer 15 years ago. She now has progressive exercise intolerance, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), ascites and swollen legs. Echocardiogram shows stiff ventricles of normal size, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function with a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy
Chemotherapy can also cause dilated cardiomyopathy, but that gives dilated, thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction. Stiff, normal-sized ventricles with big atria are restrictive.
Acute myocarditis
Myocarditis follows a recent viral prodrome with acute heart failure and raised troponin. A slow course years after radiation with stiff ventricles is restrictive disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited, with an asymmetric thick septum and outflow murmur. Treatment-related fibrosis with big atria is restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Correct. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy cause inflammation and then fibrosis that restricts filling, and a prior history of radiation or chemotherapy is a named clue in restrictive cardiomyopathy.

set1.q: A 29-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a viral illness has fluid retention with bilateral leg edema and crackles, but his blood pressure is stable. He is receiving supportive care. Which medication may be added as needed for his fluid retention?
opts: A thrombolytic drug
Thrombolytics dissolve clot and have no role in myocarditis fluid overload. A diuretic is added as needed for fluid retention.
Alcohol septal ablation
Septal ablation treats outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Fluid retention in myocarditis is managed with a diuretic.
A diuretic

Correct. Supportive care is the mainstay of myocarditis treatment, and medications are added as needed for the clinical scenario: diuretics for fluid retention, with vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation as indicated.
A positive inotrope
He is hemodynamically stable, so nothing calls for an inotrope. Fluid retention in myocarditis is treated with a diuretic as part of supportive care.

set1.q: A 23-year-old previously healthy man has breathlessness, chest pain and exercise intolerance ten days after a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea. He is tachycardic with a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) and crackles at both bases. Troponin is elevated and coronary angiography is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute viral myocarditis

Correct. Acute heart failure in an otherwise healthy young man with no cardiac history, one to two weeks after a flulike prodrome, with raised troponin and normal coronaries, is acute viral myocarditis.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy follows an emotional or physical stressor, and 90% of cases are postmenopausal women. A viral prodrome in a young man points to myocarditis.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with an outflow murmur and exertional syncope, not acute heart failure after a viral illness.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is rare, presents late with right-sided congestion, and follows infiltration, radiation or chemotherapy rather than a recent viral illness.

set1.q: A 35-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy developed severe asthma symptoms when a beta blocker was started, and it was stopped. She still has exertional breathlessness from outflow obstruction. Which medication is the appropriate alternative?
opts: Nifedipine, a vasodilator
Nifedipine is a dihydropyridine that mainly vasodilates. Lowering afterload worsens outflow obstruction; the calcium channel blockers used are verapamil and diltiazem.
Nitroglycerin paste
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload and aggravate outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Verapamil or diltiazem is the alternative.
Norepinephrine infusion
Norepinephrine is a positive inotrope that increases contractility and may induce arrhythmias, so it is avoided. The alternative to a beta blocker is verapamil or diltiazem.
Verapamil or diltiazem

Correct. The nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers verapamil and diltiazem are the listed alternative to a beta blocker for outflow tract obstruction, slowing the heart and reducing contractility.

set1.q: A 28-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without obstruction has brief runs of ventricular tachycardia on ambulatory monitoring. A defibrillator is being arranged. Which antiarrhythmic has been shown to reduce his risk of sudden cardiac death?
opts: Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin is avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because it reduces preload and afterload. It has no role in preventing sudden cardiac death; amiodarone does.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is a positive inotrope that increases contractility and may induce arrhythmias, so it is avoided. Amiodarone is the antiarrhythmic shown to reduce sudden death.
Amiodarone

Correct. Amiodarone is proven to reduce the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with or without outflow obstruction, and it also converts and suppresses atrial fibrillation and flutter.
Digoxin
Digoxin is a positive inotrope avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because it raises contractility and may induce arrhythmias. Amiodarone reduces sudden death risk.

set1.q: A 68-year-old woman has crushing chest pain and breathlessness the day after her husband's funeral. She has no hypertension, diabetes or smoking history. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation with T-wave inversion, troponin is elevated, and echocardiogram shows hypokinesis of the mid and apical segments of the left ventricle. Catheterization shows normal coronary arteries. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a progressive global dilation with reduced squeeze over months, not a sudden regional apical weakness triggered by emotional stress.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

Correct. A postmenopausal woman after an emotional stressor, with ST elevation, raised troponin, mid and apical hypokinesis and normal coronary arteries at catheterization, has Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with an outflow murmur. It does not produce transient apical hypokinesis after a stressor.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Restrictive cardiomyopathy presents late with right-sided congestion and big atria. Sudden chest pain after grief with apical hypokinesis is stress cardiomyopathy.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man has months of progressive breathlessness, abdominal swelling and bilateral pedal edema. He prefers to sit upright. Jugular venous pressure is raised and he has a Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration), hepatomegaly and ascites. His electrocardiogram shows low voltage (small complexes) in all leads, and echocardiogram shows normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Stress cardiomyopathy is a sudden, transient apical weakness after a stressor. Months of right-sided congestion with stiff ventricles and big atria is restrictive disease.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Correct. Stiff ventricles with a near-normal cavity, preserved ejection fraction and big atria, presenting late with right-sided failure, are restrictive cardiomyopathy; low voltage points to amyloidosis, the most common cause in the United States.
Dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with a reduced ejection fraction. Normal-sized ventricles with a preserved fraction and big atria are restrictive.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows asymmetric septal thickening with an outflow murmur and prominent Q waves rather than low voltage. Right-sided congestion with big atria fits restrictive disease.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy has breathlessness on exertion and peripheral edema. On examination her neck veins distend when firm pressure is held over her right upper abdomen, a sign called hepatojugular reflux (neck-vein distension with firm pressure over the liver). Which additional finding is expected with this degree of congestion?
opts: Congestive enlargement of the liver
Correct. The gastrointestinal findings of dilated cardiomyopathy are congestive hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux and ascites, all from venous congestion as the failing heart backs up blood.
A small, soft, nonpalpable liver
Venous congestion enlarges the liver rather than shrinking it. Congestive hepatomegaly sits with hepatojugular reflux and ascites in the dilated cardiomyopathy examination.
A pulsatile mass in the epigastrium
A pulsatile abdominal mass suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm, not venous congestion. With hepatojugular reflux the expected finding is congestive hepatomegaly.
Flank bruising from bleeding
Flank ecchymosis signals retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm. Venous congestion from a failing heart gives hepatomegaly and ascites instead.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure, ascites and a raised jugular venous pressure has cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to decide between restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis. Which imaging finding would point to constrictive pericarditis instead?
opts: Marked atrial enlargement
Marked enlargement of one or both atria is a feature of restrictive cardiomyopathy itself, caused by impaired ventricular filling. It does not point to pericarditis.
Preserved ejection fraction
A preserved ejection fraction until late stages is typical of restrictive cardiomyopathy, so it does not separate it from constriction. Pericardial thickening does.
Normal ventricular cavity size
A normal or near-normal cavity size is expected in restrictive cardiomyopathy. The finding that points to constrictive pericarditis is pericardial thickening.
Pericardial thickening

Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used to differentiate the two conditions, and pericardial thickening is the finding that identifies constrictive pericarditis rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy.

set1.q: A 41-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes to the emergency department with exertional chest pressure. His electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute changes, and a clinician reaches for a chest pain order set. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Nitroglycerin

Correct. Drugs that reduce preload or afterload, such as nitrates, may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so nitroglycerin should be avoided if possible in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Metoprolol
Metoprolol, a beta blocker, is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction and improves diastolic filling. It is used, not avoided.
Verapamil
Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used to treat outflow tract obstruction. The drug to avoid is a nitrate such as nitroglycerin.
Amiodarone
Amiodarone is used in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death and to control atrial fibrillation. It is not the drug to avoid.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man is newly diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by hemochromatosis, with iron deposited in the heart tissue. He has congestion and fatigue. Which is the first principle of his management?
opts: An inotrope to raise output
Systolic function is usually normal in restrictive cardiomyopathy, and an inotrope does not address the stiff filling. The first principle is treating the cause.
A high-intensity exercise program
Exercise does not treat infiltrative or storage disease of the heart. Restrictive cardiomyopathy management starts with the underlying disorder.
Treat the underlying disorder

Correct. Management of restrictive cardiomyopathy begins with treating the underlying disorder, such as iron storage in hemochromatosis, with cautious diuretics, rate-slowing drugs and anticoagulation added as needed.
Septal myectomy for relief
Myectomy relieves septal outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Restrictive disease is managed first by treating its underlying cause.

set1.q: An 86-year-old woman with end-stage cardiomyopathy has breathlessness at rest, edema and fatigue despite maximal tolerated therapy. She is not a transplant or device candidate and says she wants comfort at home. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Stop all of her symptom medicines
Palliative care actively manages dyspnea, fatigue and edema; it does not withdraw symptom relief. The step now is goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral.
Add an assist device urgently
She is not a device candidate, and her stated goal is comfort at home. Advance care planning and hospice referral match end-stage disease here.
Discuss goals of care and hospice

Correct. Palliative care in cardiomyopathy covers symptom management of dyspnea, fatigue and edema, advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, support for caregivers, and hospice referral in end-stage disease.
Refer for heart transplant listing
She is not a transplant candidate and has asked for comfort at home. End-stage cardiomyopathy in this setting calls for goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral.

set1.q: A 33-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy confirmed by echocardiography has typical findings and no plans for surgery or a device. A colleague suggests cardiac catheterization to complete the work-up. When is cardiac catheterization indicated in this condition?
opts: Always, to rule out coronary disease
Chest pain can occur without coronary disease in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and catheterization is not routine. It is kept for planned invasive therapy.
Only if the murmur is very loud
Murmur intensity varies with preload and afterload and does not decide catheterization. The indication is planned invasive therapy such as a pacemaker or surgery.
Only if surgery or a pacemaker is planned
Correct. Cardiac catheterization is not required for the diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is obtained when invasive therapy such as a pacemaker or surgery is planned.
Always, to confirm the diagnosis
Echocardiography is the typical diagnostic test of choice and confirms the diagnosis. Catheterization is not required for it.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: A 22-year-old man has breathlessness on exertion and occasional palpitations. His father has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. His pulse shows pulsus bisferiens (a double systolic peak), the apical impulse is forceful and sustained, and a fourth heart sound (a late diastolic sound just before the first heart sound) is present. Which is the typical diagnostic test of choice?
opts: Chest radiograph
The chest radiograph may be normal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and cannot confirm it. Echocardiography is the typical diagnostic test of choice.
Echocardiography

Correct. Echocardiography is the typical diagnostic test of choice for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, showing asymmetric septal hypertrophy, a small cavity, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and left atrial enlargement.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is not required for diagnosis and is obtained only when invasive therapy such as a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Echocardiography is the test of choice.
Genetic testing
Genetic testing is available but does not influence treatment, and it is not the diagnostic test of choice. Echocardiography confirms the thick left ventricular wall.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: A 55-year-old man has progressive breathlessness on exertion, fatigue and swelling of both legs. The apical impulse is displaced laterally, a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is present, and there is a soft murmur at the apex. Which echocardiogram finding would support dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Midsegment and apical hypokinesis alone
Hypokinesis confined to the mid and apical segments is the transient regional pattern of stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, not global dilation.
Dilated thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction

Correct. Dilated, thin walls are the prominent echocardiogram feature, with an ejection fraction below 40%, hypokinetic chambers, possibly all four chambers dilated, mitral or tricuspid regurgitation and sometimes thrombus.
A thick septum and a small left ventricular cavity
Asymmetric septal thickening with a small cavity is the echocardiogram of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where the ejection fraction is normal or even high.
Normal cavity size with large atria and stiff walls
A near-normal cavity with marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function is restrictive cardiomyopathy, where systolic function is usually preserved.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: A 50-year-old man is newly diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy after a viral illness. He is in sinus rhythm, blood pressure is 118/72, and his ejection fraction is 30%. No thrombus is seen on echocardiogram. Which pair of drug classes should he receive whatever the cause of his disease?
opts: Anticoagulant and antiarrhythmic started for everyone
Anticoagulation is kept for atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or a known mural thrombus, and antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone for specific rhythms. Neither is started routinely.
Verapamil and a nitrate to relax the thick ventricle
Verapamil suits the stiff or hypertrophied ventricle of restrictive or hypertrophic disease. A dilated, weak ventricle is treated with a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
A diuretic alone, until symptoms settle to baseline
Diuretics relieve sodium and water retention as an adjunct, but they are not the mortality-reducing backbone. That is the beta blocker plus angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor pair.
Beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor

Correct. Treatment of dilated cardiomyopathy is essentially that of chronic heart failure, and every patient, regardless of cause, should receive a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, both of which reduce mortality.

set1.q: A 30-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and no high-risk features wants to stay active. He used to run marathons competitively and asks what level of exercise he should aim for. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Unrestricted competitive team sports
Sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is related to extreme exertion, so unrestricted competition is not advised. Activity is kept mild to moderate and noncompetitive.
Strict bed rest for the rest of life
Complete rest is not the recommendation. Patients are encouraged toward mild to moderate recreational activity in a noncompetitive manner.
Heavy lifting to build heart strength
Strenuous exertion is what drives sudden death risk in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Mild to moderate noncompetitive activity is the counseling point.
Mild to moderate noncompetitive activity

Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have historically been told to confine themselves to mild to moderate recreational activities in a noncompetitive manner, because sudden death relates to extreme exertion.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with stress cardiomyopathy confirmed by normal coronary arteries at catheterization is stable, with no ventricular thrombus and no signs of heart failure. Which medication is described as helpful in her supportive treatment?
opts: An inotrope infusion
Nothing in her stable presentation calls for an inotrope. Supportive treatment in stress cardiomyopathy lists beta blockers as helpful.
A thrombolytic drug
Her coronary arteries are normal and there is no clot to dissolve. Beta blockers are the helpful supportive medication in Takotsubo.
Amyl nitrite by inhalation
Amyl nitrite is a bedside maneuver agent that lowers afterload to change a murmur. It is not a treatment for stress cardiomyopathy; beta blockers are.
A beta blocker

Correct. Treatment of Takotsubo is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation; beta blockers are described as helpful, with anticoagulation only for a thrombus and diuretics only for heart failure.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: A 74-year-old man with restrictive cardiomyopathy is found to have cardiac amyloidosis, with amyloid protein deposited in the heart tissue. He has breathlessness, leg edema and ascites. Which electrocardiogram finding is expected with this infiltrative disease?
opts: Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation is listed among the electrocardiogram findings of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Infiltrative amyloid disease produces low QRS voltage.
ST elevation
ST elevation with T-wave inversion is the electrocardiogram of stress cardiomyopathy. Amyloid infiltration of the heart gives low QRS voltage.
Low QRS voltage
Correct. The electrocardiogram in restrictive cardiomyopathy may show low QRS voltage in amyloidosis infiltrative disease, and atrial fibrillation and bundle branch blocks are also common.
Prominent Q waves
Prominent Q waves in the inferior and lateral leads reflect septal depolarization of hypertrophied muscle in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Amyloidosis gives low QRS voltage.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy develops a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex that radiates to the left axilla. Her ventricle has continued to enlarge on serial echocardiograms. Which complication best accounts for the new murmur?
opts: Pericardial thickening from constriction
Pericardial thickening marks constrictive pericarditis, the differential of restrictive cardiomyopathy. It does not create a holosystolic apical murmur.
Functional mitral regurgitation from dilation

Correct. As the ventricle dilates, the valve apparatus is distorted, and mitral regurgitation (which appears earlier) and tricuspid regurgitation commonly develop. The mitral murmur is holosystolic at the apex, radiating to the axilla.
Outflow obstruction from a thick septum
Septal outflow obstruction belongs to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and gives a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border that does not radiate to the axilla.
Tricuspid regurgitation into the axilla
Tricuspid regurgitation is heard at the lower left sternal border and radiates along the sternum, not to the axilla. An apical murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has pulmonary and systemic congestion, with crackles and leg edema. A diuretic is being started. Which statement about diuretic use in her is most accurate?
opts: Use with caution; stiff ventricles need preload

Correct. Diuretics are used for pulmonary and systemic congestion in restrictive cardiomyopathy, but with caution, because they lower preload and the noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output.
Contraindicated in any restrictive disease
Diuretics are not contraindicated; they treat the pulmonary and systemic congestion. They are simply used with caution because stiff ventricles need preload.
Give aggressively to fully dry the lungs
Aggressive diuresis drops the preload that stiff ventricles rely on and can collapse cardiac output. Diuretics are used, but cautiously.
Only useful once the ejection fraction falls
Diuretics treat congestion whatever the ejection fraction, which is usually preserved until late. The caution is about lowering preload.

set1.q: A 65-year-old woman developed chest pain and dyspnea during a hurricane evacuation. She has ST elevation, an elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide, and an echocardiogram showing akinesis of the left ventricular apex. Which test confirms stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: Cardiac catheterization
Correct. The diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries despite the infarct-like presentation.
Endomyocardial biopsy
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not for stress cardiomyopathy. Catheterization with normal coronary arteries confirms Takotsubo.
Exercise stress test
Exercise testing is inappropriate with active ST elevation and does not confirm the diagnosis. Cardiac catheterization with normal coronaries does.
Serial troponin levels
Troponin is usually elevated in Takotsubo, just as in a heart attack, so it cannot separate them. Catheterization showing normal coronaries confirms it.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy, sinus rhythm and an ejection fraction of 20% has a follow-up echocardiogram that shows a thrombus layered against the wall of the left ventricle. Which additional treatment is now indicated?
opts: Stop the beta blocker
A beta blocker is kept in every patient with dilated cardiomyopathy because it lowers mortality. The new thrombus calls for anticoagulation, not withdrawal of therapy.
Alcohol septal ablation
Alcohol septal ablation treats septal outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A mural thrombus in a dilated ventricle is treated with anticoagulation.
Surgical myectomy now
Myectomy removes obstructing septal muscle in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and does not address a mural thrombus, which needs anticoagulation to prevent embolism.
Start anticoagulation

Correct. Dilated ventricles carry a risk of thromboembolic complications, and a known mural thrombus is one of the three indications for anticoagulation in dilated cardiomyopathy, with atrial fibrillation and an artificial valve.

set1.q: A 16-year-old girl with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has had an episode of fainting during basketball practice and brief runs of ventricular tachycardia on monitoring. She wants to keep playing on her competitive school team. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Activity restriction given her high risk

Correct. Activity restriction for high-risk individuals is an adolescent strategy, and sudden death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is highest in preadolescents and adolescents and is related to extreme exertion.
Unrestricted play with extra fluids
Hydration is advised in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but it does not make competitive play safe for a high-risk adolescent. Activity restriction is the strategy.
Clearance once the murmur softens
The murmur varies with preload and position and says nothing about her sudden death risk. Exertional syncope and ventricular tachycardia call for activity restriction.
Competitive play on a beta blocker
A beta blocker treats outflow obstruction but does not license competitive sport in a high-risk patient. Sudden death relates to extreme exertion, so activity is restricted.

set2.q: A 20-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a flulike illness is on the ward with heart failure symptoms. He reports new palpitations, and his nurse notes a brief episode of lightheadedness. Which complication poses the most immediate threat to his life?
opts: Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is not a complication of myocarditis. The life-threatening risk behind palpitations and presyncope here is ventricular arrhythmia or heart block.
Pericardial thickening
Pericardial thickening marks constrictive pericarditis, the differential of restrictive cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis threatens life through ventricular arrhythmia.
Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse is a valve disorder unrelated to myocarditis. Palpitations with near-syncope in myocarditis signal ventricular arrhythmia or heart block.
Ventricular arrhythmia

Correct. Palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death in myocarditis are due to underlying ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, and myocarditis can cause rapidly progressive, often fatal, arrhythmia.

set2.q: A 24-year-old woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a recent viral illness is being evaluated for myocarditis. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Which laboratory result would indicate cardiac myonecrosis?
opts: Elevated serum troponin

Correct. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis in myocarditis. The rest of the work-up adds leukocytosis on the blood count, a possibly elevated sedimentation rate and electrocardiogram changes.
A low white cell count
The blood count in myocarditis shows leukocytosis, a raised rather than low white cell count, and it does not measure myocardial injury. Troponin does.
Normal sedimentation rate
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis, and in either case it does not indicate myonecrosis. Troponin is the marker of heart muscle injury.
A low natriuretic peptide
A B-type natriuretic peptide below 100 pg/mL argues against heart failure; it is not a marker of myonecrosis. Elevated troponin is.

set2.q: A 71-year-old woman admitted with stress cardiomyopathy after a house fire has a repeat echocardiogram that shows a thrombus in the akinetic left ventricular apex. She is in sinus rhythm. Which treatment is now indicated?
opts: Nitrate infusion
A nitrate infusion does not treat a ventricular thrombus. Supportive care in Takotsubo adds anticoagulation when a left ventricular thrombus is present.
Surgical myectomy
Myectomy relieves septal obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A thrombus in the akinetic apex is treated with anticoagulation.
Anticoagulation

Correct. Treatment of Takotsubo is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation: anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present, beta blockers as helpful, and diuretics if heart failure is present.
Pacemaker insertion
A pacemaker treats heart block from conduction disease, which she does not have. A left ventricular thrombus calls for anticoagulation.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy has taken a beta blocker, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, spironolactone and a diuretic for many months. She still has breathlessness on moderate exertion, and a repeat echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 25%. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator

Correct. An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is indicated when the ejection fraction stays below 35% after maximum medical therapy, because sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia is a major cause of death in dilated cardiomyopathy.
Endomyocardial biopsy to find a cause

Biopsy is not routine and rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy; it is kept for rapidly deteriorating function or systemic disease such as hemochromatosis. Her persistent low ejection fraction calls for a defibrillator.
Surgical myectomy of the septum
Myectomy removes septal muscle that obstructs outflow in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Her problem is a dilated, weak ventricle, which is treated with a defibrillator after maximal therapy.
Stopping the beta blocker
All patients with dilated cardiomyopathy should stay on a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; beta blockers reduce mortality, so stopping it would remove a proven therapy.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy and marked biatrial enlargement has had palpitations for a week, and the electrocardiogram now shows atrial fibrillation. Which treatment reduces her risk of embolism?
opts: Surgical myectomy
Myectomy removes obstructing septal muscle in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Embolism from atrial thrombi in restrictive disease is prevented with anticoagulation.
A positive inotrope
Inotropes do not prevent thromboembolism. With atrial fibrillation and big atria, anticoagulation is used to prevent embolism.
Anticoagulation

Correct. Atrial fibrillation is common in restrictive cardiomyopathy because of atrial enlargement, it raises the risk of atrial thrombus, and anticoagulants may be needed to prevent embolism from atrial thrombi.
Aggressive diuresis
Diuretics treat congestion and must be used cautiously in restrictive disease; they do nothing to prevent emboli. Anticoagulation prevents embolism from atrial thrombi.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 26-year-old man with suspected viral myocarditis has an elevated troponin and normal coronary arteries. His cardiologist wants to see how much of the heart muscle is inflamed without an invasive procedure. Which test shows the extent of inflammation?
opts: Gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
Correct. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging is part of the myocarditis work-up because the gadolinium improves visibility of the inflammation and shows its extent.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours
Ambulatory monitoring detects arrhythmias and grades sudden death risk, most notably in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It cannot show inflamed heart muscle.
Exercise echocardiography with treadmill testing
Exercise echocardiography assesses functional capacity, ischemia and obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It does not show the extent of inflammation.
Right heart catheterization with pressure tracings
Pressure tracings help evaluate restrictive physiology. Inflammation is shown noninvasively by gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman was admitted with chest pain after a near drowning. Her electrocardiogram showed ST elevation with T-wave inversion, and echocardiography showed hypokinesis of the midsegment and apex of the left ventricle. Which catheterization finding is expected if this is stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: A proximal coronary occlusion
An occluded coronary artery would mean a true myocardial infarction. The definition of Takotsubo requires the absence of angiographic coronary disease.
A ruptured coronary plaque
Acute plaque rupture is exactly what is absent in stress cardiomyopathy. Catheterization most often shows normal coronary arteries.
Triple-vessel narrowing
Severe multivessel coronary disease would point to ischemic heart disease. In Takotsubo the coronary arteries are most often normal.
Normal coronary arteries
Correct. Stress cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome but lacks angiographic coronary artery disease or acute plaque rupture; catheterization most often shows normal coronary arteries.

set2.q: A 48-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is admitted after surgery with low blood pressure, and a resident proposes a drug to strengthen her heart's contraction. Which drug class should be avoided in her?
opts: Beta blockers such as metoprolol
Beta blockers are the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, reducing contractility and improving filling. They are not the class to avoid.
Antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone
Amiodarone reduces the risk of sudden cardiac death and converts atrial fibrillation in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Positive inotropes are the class to avoid.
Calcium channel blockers like verapamil
Verapamil and diltiazem treat outflow obstruction by slowing the heart and reducing contractility. Drugs that increase contractility are the ones avoided.
Positive inotropes such as digoxin

Correct. Positive inotropes such as digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine are avoided because the increased contractility worsens outflow obstruction, raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 19-year-old woman with a week of fever and myalgia now has severe breathlessness. She is cold and clammy with a blood pressure of 78/50, heart rate 128, raised jugular venous pressure and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Exercise testing to grade severity
Exercise testing has no place in cardiogenic shock. Myocarditis this severe needs aggressive hemodynamic stabilization.
Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization

Correct. Myocarditis can present as cardiogenic shock, and although supportive care is the mainstay, treatment is directed toward the scenario and may require aggressive hemodynamic stabilization first.
Outpatient follow-up in one week
She is in cardiogenic shock, a presentation of myocarditis that can be rapidly fatal. Delay is unsafe; aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first.
Elective biopsy before any support
Biopsy can establish the diagnosis later, but it is not done before a patient in shock is stabilized. Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 32-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and outflow tract obstruction has breathlessness and chest tightness on exertion. His blood pressure is 124/78 and heart rate is 76. He takes no cardiac medication yet. Which is the initial medication for his outflow obstruction?
opts: A high-intensity loop diuretic
Diuretics lower preload and can worsen obstruction; if needed they are used with caution to avoid dehydration. The initial drug for obstruction is a beta blocker.
A beta blocker such as metoprolol

Correct. A beta blocker such as metoprolol is the initial medication for left ventricular outflow tract obstruction; it slows the heart and improves diastolic filling. Verapamil or diltiazem is the alternative.
A nitrate such as nitroglycerin
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, which aggravates outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A beta blocker comes first.
A positive inotrope such as digoxin
Positive inotropes such as digoxin increase contractility, raise the risk of ischemia and may induce arrhythmias, so they are avoided. A beta blocker is the initial drug.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 76-year-old man with restrictive cardiomyopathy from cardiac sarcoidosis has two episodes of syncope. His heart rate is 34, and the electrocardiogram shows complete heart block. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Surgical myectomy
Myectomy relieves outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and does not treat heart block. Conduction system disease needs a permanent pacemaker.
Alcohol septal ablation
Alcohol septal ablation treats septal outflow obstruction, and it can itself cause heart block. Complete heart block from nodal fibrosis needs a permanent pacemaker.
Endomyocardial biopsy
A biopsy may help find a cause when imaging and genetic testing are negative, but it does not treat symptomatic heart block. A permanent pacemaker does.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. Fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes in restrictive cardiomyopathy can lead to heart block, and a permanent pacemaker is used for this conduction system disease.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 60-year-old man has just been diagnosed with symptomatic idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25%. He asks what his long-term outlook is. Which statement about his prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Nearly all recover fully in weeks
Full recovery in most patients describes stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy carries about 50% mortality at five years.
Worst outlook of any heart muscle disease
The poorest prognosis among heart muscle diseases belongs to restrictive cardiomyopathy. Dilated cardiomyopathy is poor too, with 50% mortality at five years.
A normal life span without therapy
Dilated cardiomyopathy is progressive, with 50% mortality at five years once symptomatic, and outcome depends on response to medical therapy.
About half die within five years

Correct. Once symptoms emerge, prognosis is poor overall, with 50% mortality at five years, largely from progressive disease and sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia. The course depends on response to therapy.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with stable cardiomyopathy on full medical therapy says he tires after walking a block and feels anxious about exercising. He has no symptoms at rest. Which referral is most appropriate to improve his exercise tolerance?
opts: A competitive sports clearance clinic
Competitive sport is not the goal for a patient who tires after a block. Structured cardiac rehabilitation builds exercise tolerance and quality of life.
A cardiac rehabilitation program

Correct. Cardiac rehabilitation programs improve exercise tolerance and quality of life, with education on medication adherence, nutrition and symptom monitoring, and psychological support for chronic illness.
Hospice referral for end-stage care
Hospice referral is for end-stage cardiomyopathy. A stable patient with limited exercise tolerance is referred to cardiac rehabilitation instead.
Genetic screening of his children
Genetic screening targets hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in adolescents and families with inherited disease. It would not improve his own exercise tolerance.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has fatigue and exercise intolerance along with leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites, but her lungs are relatively clear. Which pattern of heart failure is expected to dominate in this condition?
opts: Isolated left-sided failure
Left-sided failure brings pulmonary congestion, crackles and orthopnea to the fore. In restrictive cardiomyopathy right-sided failure often dominates instead.
High-output heart failure
Restrictive cardiomyopathy reduces output because stiff ventricles fill poorly. The dominant pattern is right-sided failure, not a high-output state.
Pure systolic failure
Systolic function is usually normal in restrictive cardiomyopathy; the problem is diastolic filling, and right-sided failure tends to dominate.
Right-sided heart failure
Correct. Although filling pressures are raised in both ventricles, right heart failure is often more prominent and may dominate in restrictive cardiomyopathy, giving edema, hepatomegaly and ascites.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 17-year-old boy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy asks his clinician what the most serious risk of his disease is. He has occasional palpitations and plays recreational basketball. Which complication is the leading cause of death in this condition?
opts: Embolic stroke
Embolic stroke is a risk once atrial fibrillation develops, which is why anticoagulation is used. The leading cause of death is sudden cardiac death.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is not a complication of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The leading cause of death is sudden cardiac death, usually from ventricular fibrillation.
Sudden cardiac death

Correct. Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, highest in preadolescents and adolescents with extreme exertion, and over 80% of cases are associated with ventricular fibrillation.
Progressive heart failure
Heart failure symptoms gradually progress in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but sudden cardiac death, mostly from ventricular fibrillation, is the leading cause of mortality.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with suspected restrictive cardiomyopathy has right-sided heart failure and big atria on echocardiogram. Her cardiologist wants to measure pressures inside both ventricles to characterize the filling problem. Which invasive test evaluates ventricular pressure tracings?
opts: Exercise echocardiography
Exercise echocardiography assesses functional capacity and obstruction, mainly in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Ventricular pressure tracings need catheterization.
Cardiac catheterization

Correct. Cardiac catheterization is useful in restrictive cardiomyopathy to evaluate ventricular pressure tracings, alongside cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and, when needed, endomyocardial biopsy.
Endomyocardial biopsy
Biopsy samples tissue to confirm or exclude a diagnosis; it does not record pressure tracings. Catheterization measures ventricular pressures.
Transesophageal echocardiogram
Transesophageal echocardiography images the valves and chambers with ultrasound but does not record direct ventricular pressure tracings. Cardiac catheterization does.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 60-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), crackles at both lung bases and diminished breath sounds at the right base. A chest radiograph is ordered. Which finding on the film would indicate pulmonary edema?
opts: Short horizontal lines meeting the pleura

Correct. Kerley B lines are horizontal lines 1 to 2 cm long that meet the pleura at right angles and indicate pulmonary edema. Cardiomegaly and pleural effusions are the other expected radiograph findings.
A small heart with clear lung fields
Dilated cardiomyopathy shows cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and pulmonary edema on the chest radiograph. A small heart with clear lungs would argue against congestion.
A normal film that excludes congestion
The radiograph in dilated cardiomyopathy is expected to show cardiomegaly and effusions, and edema may show as Kerley B lines. A normal film would not fit his crackles.
Isolated thickening of the pericardium
Pericardial thickening is the imaging clue to constrictive pericarditis, and it is shown on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging rather than as the sign of pulmonary edema.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 45-year-old man presents with new-onset heart failure a week after a flulike illness. He smokes and has hyperlipidemia, so the team wants to exclude coronary disease before labeling this myocarditis. Which test rules out coronary ischemia as the cause of his new heart failure?
opts: Sedimentation rate
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis but is nonspecific and cannot exclude coronary disease. Angiography does.
Chest radiograph
The chest radiograph is nonspecific and may show cardiomegaly, but it cannot show the coronary arteries. Cardiac angiography rules out ischemia.
Cardiac angiography
Correct. Cardiac angiography is used in the myocarditis work-up to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new-onset heart failure, which matters in a patient with coronary risk factors.
Endomyocardial biopsy
Biopsy is the gold standard for confirming myocarditis once other causes are excluded, but it does not image the coronary arteries. Angiography rules out ischemia.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 64-year-old man has restrictive cardiomyopathy confirmed on imaging, but cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and genetic testing have not identified a cause. His team is considering endomyocardial biopsy. When is biopsy performed in this condition?
opts: Only after cardiac transplantation is done
Biopsy is used during the diagnostic work-up, when imaging and genetic testing are negative, not only after transplantation.
Never, since it cannot change management
Biopsy is performed precisely when a tissue sample could confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management, after negative imaging and genetic tests.
When imaging and genetic tests are negative

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is performed when all imaging studies and genetic testing are negative, or when a tissue sample is likely to confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management.
As the first test in every suspected case
Biopsy is not the first test; echocardiography, electrocardiogram and radiograph come first, then cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Biopsy follows negative imaging and genetic testing.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: A 47-year-old man has new dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30%. He reports fatigue, heat intolerance and weight loss, and the conjunctivae look pale. Which initial laboratory tests are most useful for finding a contributing cause?
opts: Blood cultures and a throat swab
Cultures do not appear in the dilated cardiomyopathy laboratory panel. The panel looks for anemia, electrolyte and renal problems, liver disease and thyroid dysfunction.
Urine osmolality and cortisol
Neither test is part of the listed work-up. Anemia is checked with a blood count and thyroid dysfunction with thyroid function tests, alongside metabolic and liver panels.
Thyroid function and a blood count

Correct. The initial laboratory work-up for dilated cardiomyopathy includes a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel, liver function and thyroid function. His symptoms point to thyroid disease and anemia.
Serum lipase and amylase levels
Pancreatic enzymes are not part of the dilated cardiomyopathy work-up. The listed tests are a blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel, liver function and thyroid function.

set2.q: A 26-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is leaving for a summer hiking trip in a hot climate. She takes a beta blocker and asks how to lower her risk of symptoms while away. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Take extra diuretic on hot days
Diuretics lower preload and can aggravate outflow obstruction; they are used with caution to avoid dehydration. Extra doses in the heat would be dangerous.
Use alcohol to relax at the campsite
Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are taught to avoid excess alcohol consumption, alongside keeping well hydrated and avoiding competitive exertion.
Stay well hydrated; avoid dehydration
Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should maintain hydration, because dehydration lowers preload and worsens outflow obstruction; diuretics are used with caution for the same reason.
Restrict fluids to soften the murmur
Fluid restriction reduces preload, which worsens obstruction and makes the murmur louder. Education is to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration.

set2.q: A 73-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis. She has right-sided heart failure and asks how her condition compares with other kinds of heart muscle disease. Which statement about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Poorest of all heart muscle diseases
Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis among all types of heart muscle disease, and it often presents at an advanced stage with pronounced cardiopulmonary symptoms.
Complete recovery within weeks
Complete recovery in most patients is the course of stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis of all heart muscle diseases.
A normal life span with diuretics
Diuretics relieve congestion but do not change the outlook, which is the poorest among heart muscle diseases. Transplantation is an option in advanced disease.
Better than other cardiomyopathies
Restrictive cardiomyopathy carries the poorest prognosis among heart muscle diseases rather than a better one, partly because it presents late.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man has right-sided heart failure with a raised jugular venous pressure and ascites. Echocardiogram shows abnormal diastolic filling, normal-sized ventricles and big atria, but the team cannot tell restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis. Which test is used to differentiate them?
opts: Ambulatory rhythm monitoring
Rhythm monitoring detects arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation but cannot image the pericardium. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging differentiates the two.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging

Correct. Echocardiography alone is not definitive because restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis look alike; cardiac magnetic resonance imaging differentiates them by showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis.
Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram
Echocardiography alone is not definitive for this distinction, so repeating it adds little. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging shows the pericardial thickening that settles it.
Exercise stress echocardiogram
Exercise echocardiography is used for functional capacity and obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging separates restriction from constriction.

set2.q: A 15-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical. He has no symptoms, but his father was recently diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Which strategy for this adolescent is most appropriate?
opts: Genetic screening for the condition

Correct. Age-specific strategies for adolescents include genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and disease detected in a family member is a common reason evaluation begins. One affected parent is enough to pass it on.
Waiting until adulthood to evaluate
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden death in preadolescents and adolescents, so evaluation should not wait. Genetic screening is the adolescent strategy.
A routine chest radiograph each year
The chest radiograph may be normal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is not a screening tool. Adolescents with an affected parent get genetic screening.
An endomyocardial biopsy at this visit
Biopsy has no role in screening relatives. The adolescent strategy for a family history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is genetic screening.

set2.q: A 59-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has just undergone alcohol septal ablation, in which alcohol is injected through a catheter into a septal branch of the coronary artery. He asks when he can expect his symptoms to improve. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Never; it is a diagnostic test
Alcohol septal ablation is a treatment for outflow obstruction, not a diagnostic test. The septum thins over months after the therapeutic infarction.
Over months as the septum thins
Correct. Alcohol septal ablation induces a therapeutic infarction of the proximal septum, and it takes months for the septum to thin and the outflow obstruction to ease.
Within minutes of the injection
The ablation creates a controlled infarction of septal muscle, and the benefit comes as the septum thins, which takes months rather than minutes.
Only after a repeat injection
A repeat procedure is not routine; the effect develops over months as the infarcted septal muscle thins. Reintervention is needed in a minority of patients.

set2.q: A 38-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy still has disabling breathlessness despite a beta blocker and later verapamil. Echocardiogram shows systolic anterior motion (the anterior mitral leaflet pulled into the outflow tract) with mitral regurgitation. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Permanent pacemaker alone
A permanent pacemaker treats conduction disease such as heart block. Refractory outflow obstruction is relieved by removing septal muscle with myectomy or alcohol septal ablation.
Long-term nitrate therapy
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload and aggravate outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided. Refractory obstruction goes on to septal reduction by myectomy.
Escalating loop diuretics
Diuretics lower preload and can worsen obstruction; they are used only with caution. Symptoms refractory to medication are treated with septal myectomy.
Surgical septal myectomy

Correct. Surgical myectomy excises part of the septal myocardium causing outflow obstruction, and the mitral regurgitation from systolic anterior motion may resolve with myectomy alone, without valve replacement.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has new palpitations. Her pulse is irregularly irregular and the electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation. Echocardiogram shows left atrial enlargement. Which treatment prevents embolic stroke in her?
opts: Anticoagulation

Correct. Atrial fibrillation in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is treated with anticoagulation to prevent embolic stroke, together with antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone and, where needed, radiofrequency ablation.
Digoxin for rate control
Digoxin is a positive inotrope that is avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because it increases contractility. Stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation is anticoagulation.
Nitrate therapy
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, aggravate outflow obstruction and do nothing to prevent emboli. Anticoagulation prevents embolic stroke in atrial fibrillation.
Diuretic therapy
Diuretics are used only with caution in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and do not prevent thromboembolism. Anticoagulation is the stroke-prevention step.

set2.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. His father had a cardiomyopathy and his older brother died suddenly at 35. No alcohol, drug or chemotherapy exposure is found. Which is the most appropriate referral for him and his family?
opts: Family screening only after age 60
Most dilated cardiomyopathy presents between 20 and 60, and his brother died at 35. Waiting until 60 would come too late; genetic counseling is indicated now.
Genetic counseling for the family

Correct. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy accounts for up to 35% of cases, usually autosomal dominant, and genetic counseling is part of patient education when there is a family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death.
Reassurance that it is not inherited
A family history of cardiomyopathy and sudden death is a red flag for familial disease, which is common and usually autosomal dominant. Reassurance would miss relatives at risk.
Heart biopsies for his relatives
Biopsy is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy and is not a family screening tool. The step for a positive family history is genetic counseling.

set2.q: A 79-year-old man with cardiomyopathy has become lightheaded on standing since his medications were increased at his last visit. He is frail and has lost weight. Which parts of his drug therapy call for particular caution at his age?
opts: Diuretics and vasodilators

Correct. Age-specific strategies for elderly patients with cardiomyopathy call for cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, with therapy tailored to comorbidity and frailty and a focus on symptom control.
Sodium restriction advice
Sodium restriction is a lifestyle measure, not a drug, and it is part of adult cardiomyopathy care. The medications singled out for caution in the elderly are diuretics and vasodilators.
Home-based rehabilitation
Home-based rehabilitation is recommended for elderly or mobility-limited patients and is not a drug. Caution in the elderly applies to diuretics and vasodilators.
Implanted device checks
Device follow-up is not the concern here. His lightheadedness after medication changes fits the elderly caution about diuretics and vasodilators.

set2.q: A 46-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 20 years has six months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). The apical impulse is displaced laterally and a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25%, and coronary angiography shows no significant narrowing. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Stress cardiomyopathy
Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy is a transient regional weakness of the mid and apical segments after a stressor, mostly in postmenopausal women, not a slow global dilation over months.
Dilated cardiomyopathy

Correct. Dilation and impaired contraction without severe coronary disease or pressure or volume overload define dilated cardiomyopathy, and long-term excess alcohol is one of its named causes. The displaced apical impulse and third heart sound fit a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows a thick, often asymmetric septum with a small cavity and a normal or high ejection fraction, not thin, dilated walls with an ejection fraction of 25%.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Restrictive cardiomyopathy keeps a near-normal cavity size and systolic function with stiff walls and big atria. Dilated, thin walls with poor squeeze are the dilated pattern instead.
